query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor addition (~2 at.%) of boron into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, using arc melting and an optimized aging heat treatment to promote the in situ formation of nanoscale boride precipitates, will reinforce the alloy’s matrix and arrest crack propagation while preserving the intrinsic caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy that exhibits a large caloric effect in applied magnetic and pressure fields but suffers from poor mechanical integrity and crack formation.
generation.intervention: Add approximately 2 at.% boron during synthesis by arc melting, followed by an aging heat treatment designed to induce the formation of fine, uniformly distributed boride precipitates.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted near the caloric transition temperature (~300 K) under applied magnetic fields (~2 T) and pressure fields (up to ~50 MPa), with compressive loading conditions matching those used in prior evaluations of epoxy- and low-melting In–composites.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale boride precipitates that form within the alloy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The boride precipitates act to pin and blunt crack tips, thereby arresting crack propagation. This dispersion strengthening improves the alloy’s compressive strength and fracture toughness without significantly disrupting the magneto-structural phase transition responsible for the caloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should exhibit a significant improvement in mechanical integrity—anticipated as a 20–30% increase in compressive strength and enhanced crack resistance—while the caloric response (e.g., entropy change) remains within ±10% of that in the unchanged alloy.
generation.baseline: The original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which shows high caloric performance but suffers from inadequate mechanical integrity (e.g., compressive strengths in the range of 152–218 MPa from comparable MM′X formulations with epoxy or low-melting In composites).
generation.boundary: This outcome is expected under operational conditions near 300 K with applied magnetic fields of ~2 T, pressure fields up to ~50 MPa, and under compressive loading environments similar to those in previous studies. The synthesis must remain rare‐earth–free.
generation.uncertainty: Exact improvements in strength and the precise limits of the caloric effect preservation will depend on fine-tuning the boron content and heat treatment parameters. Quantitative improvements need to be verified experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: a control group of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy without boron and an experimental group with ~2 at.% boron addition. Use arc melting followed by identical aging heat treatments for both sets. Test both groups under applied magnetic field (~2 T) and pressure (~50 MPa) at ~300 K.
measurements: Compressive strength and fracture toughness (to assess crack propagation resistance)
Caloric response (e.g., entropy change under applied fields)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the boron-enhanced samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (≥20% increase) in compressive strength and crack resistance relative to the control while maintaining a caloric response within ±10% of that of the unchanged alloy.

chosen.why: This intervention directly fills the identified gap by reinforcing the alloy matrix via in situ nanostructured boride precipitates that arrest crack propagation while leaving the magneto-structural (caloric) phase transition intact. It thus promises to achieve the desired coexistence of robust mechanical integrity and high caloric performance under the specified operational conditions, and it employs standard synthesis techniques without the use of rare-earth elements. A decisive controlled experiment comparing the compressive strength and caloric response of the boron‐enhanced alloy to the unchanged alloy would falsify the hypothesis if the precipitate formation either compromises the caloric effect or fails to improve strength.
